## Overview

Dune: Imperium is a deck-building worker-placement game. Each player leads a Great House of the Landsraad: you play cards to send Agents to board spaces, use Persuasion to acquire new cards for your deck, recruit and deploy troops to fight over each round's Conflict card, and climb the Influence tracks of four Factions (Emperor, Spacing Guild, Bene Gesserit, Fremen), earning Alliances. Successes are measured in Victory Points. At the end of any round in which a player has reached 10 or more VP (or the Conflict Deck is empty), the game ends and whoever has the most Victory Points wins.

Each Leader has two unique abilities: one used during play as described on the Leader, and a Signet Ring ability activated when you play your Signet Ring card on one of your Agent turns. Note: cards of any type can override the usual rules of the game.

**Scope:** original 2020 Dune: Imperium base game, standard 2–4-player multiplayer. Two-player play requires one House Hagal Rival (see below). Solo play, optional variants, expansions and Dune: Imperium — Uprising rules are excluded. Clarifications incorporate the official January 13, 2025 FAQ where applicable to this base game.

## Components

- Game board
- 8 Leaders (two each from four Great Houses), with a Turn Sequence guide on their backs. Leaders have 1-3 icons after their names; more icons = more strategically complex.
- 67 Imperium Deck cards
- 24 Reserve cards: 8 Arrakis Liaison, 10 The Spice Must Flow, 6 Foldspace
- 40 Intrigue cards
- 18 Conflict cards: 4 Conflict I, 10 Conflict II, 4 Conflict III
- Solari tokens: 4 large (worth 5), 20 small (worth 1)
- Spice tokens: 3 large (worth 5), 20 small (worth 1)
- 15 water tokens
- 4 Alliance tokens, First Player marker, Mentat (a freelance Agent pawn)
- 4 Baron Harkonnen tokens (used only with the Baron Vladimir Harkonnen Leader)
- Board Space Guide sheet; House Hagal rules sheet and 31 House Hagal cards (used only in solo and two-player games)
- Per player, in their color: 3 Agents, 3 Control markers, 1 Combat marker, a 10-card starting deck, 16 cubes (4 become Influence markers; the other 12 are your troops), 2 discs — 1 Score marker and 1 Councilor token

**Starting deck (10 cards, identical for all players):** Convincing Argument x2, Dagger x2, Dune the Desert Planet x2, Diplomacy, Reconnaissance, Seek Allies, Signet Ring.

## Setup

1. Place the game board. Place the Mentat on its side in the Mentat space, and the 4 Alliance tokens on the marked areas of the four Factions' Influence tracks.
2. Build the face-down 10-card Conflict Deck using **three separately shuffled tiers**. Its final order from **top to bottom** is: **1 card randomly dealt from the shuffled 4 Conflict I cards; 5 cards randomly dealt from the shuffled 10 Conflict II cards; all 4 Conflict III cards in shuffled order**. Shuffle every tier before taking its cards. Return the unused Conflict cards to the box without looking at them.
3. Prepare the card areas along the board edge. **Intrigue Deck:** shuffle it and place it **face down**. **Imperium Deck and Row:** shuffle the deck, place it **face down**, then deal **5 cards face up** for the Row. **Reserve:** place **Arrakis Liaison**, **The Spice Must Flow**, and **Foldspace** in **three separate stacks beside the Row**, one stack per named type.
4. Each player takes a Leader (chosen or random) and all components of one color. First-game recommendation: everyone uses a one-icon Leader (Paul Atreides, Glossu "The Beast" Rabban, Earl Memnon Thorvald, or Count Ilban Richese).
5. Each player places 2 Agents on their Leader and sets their third Agent (their Swordmaster) next to the game board. **Your starting deck:** shuffle your own standard **10 cards** and place the deck **face down in your supply, to the left of your Leader**.
6. Each player places one of their two discs on the Score track: on the **1** space in a 4-player game, otherwise on the **0** space. Place your Combat marker (correct side face up) on the 0 space of the Combat track.
7. Each player places 4 cubes, one each, on the bottom spaces of the four Factions' Influence tracks. The other 12 cubes are your troops: place 3 in the circular garrison on the board closest to you, and the rest in your supply along with your remaining components, in clear view of all players.
8. Each player takes 1 water. Create a bank next to the board with the Solari, spice, and remaining water tokens (these are not limited; substitute if you run out).
9. **Initial First Player:** choose one randomly and **give that player the First Player marker**. For two-player play, also set up House Hagal as described below.

## Turn Structure

The game is played in rounds, each with five phases in this order: **1. Round Start, 2. Player Turns, 3. Combat, 4. Makers, 5. Recall.**

### Phase 1: Round Start
- Reveal a new Conflict card from the top of the Conflict Deck and place it face up next to the deck (on top of Conflict cards from previous rounds).
- Each player draws 5 cards from their own deck to form their hand for the round.

### Phase 2: Player Turns
Starting with the holder of the First Player marker and continuing clockwise, players take **one turn at a time**. On your turn, take either an **Agent turn** or a **Reveal turn**. Generally you take Agent turns until you run out of Agents, then take a Reveal turn — but Agent turns are optional: you may take your Reveal turn while you still have Agents left. Once you have taken a Reveal turn, your turns are skipped for the rest of the phase; the phase ends when all players have taken a Reveal turn.

You may play Plot Intrigue cards during this phase, at any point during one of your own Agent or Reveal turns.

**Agent turn** — play one card from your hand face up, using it to send one Agent from your Leader to an unoccupied board space:
- The board space must show (in its upper-left corner) an icon matching one of the Agent icons on the card. You must choose only one Agent icon on the card; one card can't send multiple Agents. A card with no Agent icons can't be played on an Agent turn — it can only be revealed during a Reveal turn.
- You can't send an Agent to a board space that already has an Agent on it.
- You must pay any costs and meet any requirements of the space. Costs are paid immediately, before resolving any effects of the space or the played card; if you can't pay, you can't send your Agent there.
- Gain the effects of the board space, the card's **Agent box**, and the one-space Influence advancement for a Faction space **in any order**, after paying the entry cost (ignore the card's Reveal box).
- Arrows mean cost (left of / above the arrow) then effect (right of / below it). An optional arrow effect can be paid and resolved **once**, never repeated by paying again. You may decline the payment and its effect on an ordinary card; board entry costs must be paid to enter, and an Intrigue card's costs and conditions must be met to play it. Most other board/card effects are mandatory unless they say “may,” use an optional arrow, or use the optional black-X trash icon. **Standalone black-X trashing is optional; trashing used to pay a cost is required to obtain that cost’s effect.** A non-arrow instruction to trash the card itself is mandatory.
- **Recruiting:** each troop icon recruits one troop — take it from your supply and place it in your garrison. (If your supply is out of troops, you can't recruit more until some return.)
- **Deploying:** troops sitting in your garrison can't earn rewards. Only when you send an Agent to a **Combat space** may you deploy troops to the Conflict area (the center of the garrisons): any or all troops you recruited this turn (from any source, including the board space, played card and Intrigue cards), **plus up to two more troops from your garrison**. You cannot re-recruit garrison troops to evade that limit. Recruited troops you don't deploy go to your garrison as usual.

**Reveal turn** — taken when you have no Agents left (or choose not to use remaining Agents). Four steps, in order:
1. **Reveal Cards:** reveal all cards remaining in your hand, face up, kept separate from cards you played on Agent turns.
2. **Resolve Reveal Effects:** gain the effects in the **Reveal boxes** of the cards you just revealed (not of cards played during Agent turns earlier this round), in any order. A card drawn during your Reveal turn must immediately be revealed and used in that turn; it cannot become an Agent turn. Cards drawn after your Reveal turn stay in your hand for next round, when you still draw five additional cards. You may spend Persuasion to acquire new cards before, between, or after your Reveal effects (see Actions).
3. **Set Strength:** total your strength for this round's Combat — each of your troops in the Conflict is worth **2 strength**; each sword you revealed during your Reveal turn is worth **1 strength**. Troops in your garrison or supply contribute nothing. You must have at least one troop in the Conflict to have any strength: if your last troop is ever removed, your strength becomes 0 and can't be increased by any means, including swords. Announce your total and move your Combat marker to that space of the Combat track (if over 20, flip the marker to its +20 side and start again from the beginning of the track).
4. **Clean Up:** put all the cards in front of you (from your Agent and Reveal turns) into your discard pile.

A normal Reveal turn has no deployment step, but **specific card effects can deploy troops**. For example, Sardaukar Legion’s Reveal box deploys up to three troops from your garrison to the Conflict. Resolve that effect during Reveal effects, before Set Strength, so those troops count toward your strength immediately. Ordinary Agent-turn deployment still requires a Combat space; card and Control effects provide their stated exceptions.

### Phase 3: Combat
- **Combat Intrigue cards:** starting with the First Player and continuing clockwise, each player **with at least one troop in the Conflict** may play any number of Combat Intrigue cards, or pass. You are not required to pass just because you passed earlier in the phase. Once all players involved in Combat pass consecutively, resolve the Combat. If a card changes a player's troops in the Conflict (or otherwise alters strength), adjust their Combat marker — remember, with no troops in the Conflict your strength is 0. A few Combat Intrigue cards trigger "when you win a Conflict": play those only after you've won, before moving to the next phase.
- **Resolve Combat:** rewards from the Conflict card are given by strength as shown on the Combat track. Highest strength wins the Conflict and gains the top reward; second-highest gains the second reward; **in a 4-player game only**, an ordinary third-place finisher gains the third reward. A player with 0 strength receives no reward.
- **Ties:** tied for first place — no one wins the Conflict; each tied player receives the **second** reward (in a 4-player game, if two players tie for first, the other two still compete for the third reward). Tied for second — each receives the third reward, **including in two- and three-player games**; this differs from an ordinary third-place finish. Tied for third — nothing. “When you win a Conflict” effects cannot be used on a first-place tie because nobody won. If a win-trigger Intrigue is itself drawn as a victory reward, you may play it immediately.
- Once all rewards are given, each player takes their troops from the Conflict and puts them in their **supply (not their garrison)**. Reset all Combat markers to 0.

### Phase 4: Makers
Check each of the three board spaces with a Maker icon: The Great Flat, Hagga Basin, and Imperial Basin. If a space has no Agent on it, place 1 spice from the bank on it as bonus spice, adding to any bonus spice already accumulated there from previous rounds.

### Phase 5: Recall
- If any player is at **10 or more Victory Points** on the Score track, or the **Conflict Deck is empty**, the Endgame is triggered (see Scoring / Victory Conditions).
- If no one has won, prepare the next round: return the Mentat to its designated space in the Landsraad (if it isn't already there); players recall their Agents, returning them to their Leaders; pass the First Player marker clockwise; begin a new round with Phase 1. At the start of the next round, the winner of Sort Through the Chaos takes the Mentat as its Conflict reward (official FAQ timing).

## Actions

### Agent icons
Seven Agent icons appear on cards and board spaces: **Emperor, Spacing Guild, Bene Gesserit, Fremen, Landsraad, City, Spice Trade**. A card's icons determine where it can send your Agent — e.g., Sardaukar Legion's Emperor icon reaches either of the two Emperor spaces, while its Landsraad icon instead reaches one of the five Landsraad board spaces (the Mentat's designated space is in the Landsraad). Each Faction has one board space with a cost and one without.

### Board spaces
Sending an Agent to a Faction's space also gains 1 Influence with that Faction (included below).

The complete list of **Combat spaces** is: Arrakeen, Carthag, Sietch Tabr, Research Station, Imperial Basin, Hagga Basin, The Great Flat, Heighliner, Hardy Warriors and Stillsuits. Each has a desert illustration and crossed swords. Other spaces, including Conspire and Rally Troops, do not normally allow deployment.

### Acquiring cards
Persuasion gained during a round is used during your **Reveal turn** to acquire new cards: any of the five cards in the Imperium Row, or Arrakis Liaison or The Spice Must Flow from the Reserve. (Foldspace requires an acquire-Foldspace icon, normally from the Foldspace board space; it cannot be bought with Persuasion.) A card's cost is shown at its top right. Acquire as many cards as you can afford; you may pool Persuasion from multiple sources (cards and board spaces) for one card, and may split Persuasion from a single source across different cards. Persuasion can never be saved — whatever you don't use during your Reveal turn is lost. Acquired cards go to your discard pile (face up, to the right of your Leader); you don't use them right away. The Imperium Row must always have five cards: refill it immediately from the Imperium Deck, so after acquiring a card you may also acquire its replacement if you can afford it. Some cards have an **Acquire box** beneath their cost: gain that effect one time, at the moment you acquire the card (not later when you play it).

### Trashing cards
A direction to **discard** means a card from your hand unless otherwise specified; it goes to your discard pile. Trashing permanently removes a card — from your hand, your discard pile, or in play — to the game box for the rest of the game (Reserve cards are returned to their Reserve stack instead). Trashing is optional unless it's paying a cost or a card directs you to trash itself.

### Intrigue cards
Intrigue cards can provide resources, Influence, or even Victory Points. You receive them primarily from three board spaces — Carthag, Conspire, and Secrets — plus card effects showing the Intrigue card icon. Keep them face down, separate from your deck; you may look at them at any time and reveal them only when played. After a played Intrigue card resolves, discard it face up next to the Intrigue Deck. If the Intrigue deck is exhausted, shuffle its discards into a new deck. A Plot card whose effect applies at your next Reveal turn (such as Charisma or Recruitment Mission) can be played on your Agent turn: leave it face up until that Reveal turn, use it then, and discard it. Three types:
- **Plot** — play any time during one of your own Agent or Reveal turns.
- **Combat** — play only during Combat.
- **Endgame** — play only at the end of the game.

A card offering alternatives separated by **“OR”** lets you choose one effect, not combine both. For example, Master Tactician offers **3 swords OR retreat up to 3 troops** from the Conflict to your garrison; one play gives one of those options.


## Scoring / Victory Conditions

- Whenever you gain or lose a Victory Point, move your Score marker up or down one space on the Score track.
- **Game end trigger:** at the end of a round (Phase 5: Recall), if any player has reached **10 or more Victory Points**, or the **Conflict Deck is empty**, the game ends.
- **Endgame:** first, players may play and resolve any Endgame Intrigue cards they have. Then whoever has the most Victory Points is declared the winner.
- **Tiebreakers, in order:** amount of **spice**, then **Solari**, then **water**, then **garrisoned troops** (troops in your garrison on the board — not troops in your supply), then the player who **most recently took a Reveal turn**. You can score above 12 VP; the end of the printed Score track is not a limit.
- **VP sources include:** Conflict card rewards; reaching 2 Influence with a Faction (1 VP each — lost again if you drop back below 2); Alliance tokens (worth the VP shown on the token, and transferable — see below); and card effects, notably Intrigue cards (including Endgame Intrigue at game end).

## Special Rules & Edge Cases

- **Faction Influence:** your cube starts at the bottom of each track. Sending an Agent to a Faction's board space gains 1 Influence with that Faction; other effects can move you up (or occasionally down). At **2 Influence** you gain a VP (lost if you drop below 2, regained if you reach 2 again). Each track has six spaces; 3 Influence is the space immediately above the 2-Influence VP space. At **4 Influence** you earn the bonus shown on that space of the track; you do *not* give the bonus back if you later drop below 4, and you can even earn it again by dropping back and re-advancing.
- **Alliances:** the **first** player to reach 4 Influence with a Faction takes its Alliance token and gains the VP shown on it. If an opponent ever passes them by rising to a **higher** space on that track, the token (and its VP) transfers to that opponent. Merely tying the holder does not take it. If the holder loses Influence while previously tied with another player, the previously tied player takes it; if several were tied, the holder chooses one. The holder also loses the token if falling to 3 Influence or less: if no player has 4 or more to take it, return it to the board. Every Alliance ownership change immediately moves **both** affected scores: the former holder loses its 1 VP and the new holder gains 1 VP; returning it to the board just loses the former holder's VP.
- **Mentat:** a freelance Agent. Take it only from its space on the board (you can't take it from another player or another space), place it on your Leader, and use it as one of your Agents this round; return it to its Landsraad space during Recall. For the Sort Through the Chaos Conflict reward, take the Mentat at the start of the next round and use it that round (official FAQ timing).
- **Swordmaster & High Council** are once-per-game spaces for each player (8 Solari for your third Agent; 5 Solari for a Council seat granting 2 Persuasion every Reveal turn).
- **Control:** some Conflict cards (titled for Arrakeen, Carthag, or Imperial Basin) reward control of that space. If you win such a Conflict, place a Control marker on the flag below that space (replacing any opponent's marker). While it's there, you receive the bonus whenever **any** player, including yourself, sends an Agent there: 1 Solari for Arrakeen or Carthag, 1 spice for Imperial Basin. **Defensive bonus:** when a Conflict card is revealed for a space you already control, you may deploy one troop **from your supply** to the Conflict.
- **Deck exhaustion:** any time you're unable to draw because your deck is empty, reshuffle your discard pile to form a new deck, then continue drawing. You can't reshuffle early — e.g., Paul Atreides' ability or Poison Snooper can't look at the top card of an empty deck.
- **Recall effects:** return the recalled Agent to your Leader; you may use it on another Agent turn in the same round. This does not reopen turns after your Reveal turn.
- **Losing vs. retreating troops:** a **lost** troop returns to your supply (not your garrison); a **retreated** troop moves from the Conflict back to your garrison. If an effect permits retreating “any number,” zero is allowed.
- **In play / Fremen Bond:** cards you play on Agent turns and reveal on your Reveal turn stay face up "in play" until your Clean Up (unless trashed first). Fremen Bond effects work if you have at least one *other* Fremen card in play; two Fremen Bond cards activate one another regardless of the order played.
- **Conditional icons:** Alliance-icon effects require holding that Faction's Alliance token; Influence-requirement icons need at least the shown Influence with that Faction. A single “gain two Influence” effect cannot be split between Factions. This differs from separate listed choices: Machinations’ first-place reward says “Choose two” of four Faction gain-one icons, so choose two different Factions and gain 1 Influence with each; do not select the same option twice.
- **Steal Intrigue:** each opponent with four or more Intrigue cards must give you one, selected at random.
- **Rulebook clarifications:**
  - *Bindu Suspension:* play at the start of your Agent turn, before anything else; draw a card, then immediately end your turn.
  - *Calculated Hire:* can only take the Mentat from its starting position in the Landsraad.
  - *Demand Respect:* if you win a Conflict that rewards spice, you may take that spice first and use it to play this card (To the Victor… can likewise fund it).
  - *Kwisatz Haderach:* lets you take an Agent turn with no Agents left by sending an Agent already on a board space (even back to the same space). It can't reuse once-per-game spaces (High Council, Swordmaster) and can't overcome The Voice.
  - *Maker spaces:* if an Agent moves away from a Maker space and it's still empty in Phase 4, bonus spice does accumulate there.
  - *Opponent discards — Test of Humanity and Reverend Mother Mohiam:* affected opponents choose which card(s) to discard **from their own hands**, not randomly. Resolve opponents starting from your left and proceeding clockwise. For Test of Humanity, each must choose something they can actually do: no discarding from an empty hand and no losing a deployed troop they do not have.
  - *The Voice:* mark the chosen board space with one of your available Control markers and remove it on your next turn; it stops opponents (including via Kwisatz Haderach) from sending Agents there for one turn.
  - *Baron Vladimir Harkonnen (Masterstroke):* after completing all setup and before the first round, secretly choose two of the four Baron Harkonnen tokens and place them Faction-side down on your Leader; return the other two to the box unseen; reveal later as described to gain your reward, only once per game.
### Two-player House Hagal Rival

House Hagal is a third, spoiler Rival in every standard two-player game. It does not collect resources, build an Imperium deck, earn Conflict rewards or score VP, and cannot claim Control. It can take and hold Faction Alliances, denying their VP to humans. It is affected by effects targeting opponents or players if it has the specified resources.

**Setup:** choose an unused color. Put one of its cubes at the bottom of each of the four Influence tracks; all remaining cubes go in its supply, with **no troops in its garrison**. Remove the three Arrakeen cards marked “1P,” shuffle the remaining House Hagal cards and put the deck and its **three Agents** near its supply. No Rival Leader or solo difficulty rules are used.

## FAQ & Rulings

These clarifications apply to the original base game; expansions, promo additions and Uprising-specific clauses of the shared FAQ are excluded.

- **Duke Leto Atreides:** Landsraad Popularity reduces by 1 Solari the entry cost of a **Landsraad (green)** board space when he sends an Agent there; apply the discount before paying to enter. It does not discount City or other space categories. His Signet Ring ability, Prudent Diplomacy, optionally pays **1 spice** for 1 Influence with a Faction where **an opponent has more Influence than Leto**; a tie without an opponent ahead is not eligible.
- **Mentat reward:** for Sort Through the Chaos, take the Mentat **at the start of the next round**. It is available as an Agent that round.
- **Assassination Mission / Imperial Spy:** Assassination Mission provides no way to trash itself for its 4 Solari; another effect must trash it. Imperial Spy draws an Intrigue only when you use its own self-trash effect, not when another effect trashes it.
- **The Spice Must Flow / Guild Bankers:** keep the VP gained for acquiring The Spice Must Flow even if you later trash it. Guild Bankers’ discount applies to **each** copy you acquire that turn.
- **Corner the Market:** at Endgame, its two conditions score independently: gain **1 VP for having at least two The Spice Must Flow cards**, and a separate **1 VP for having more than each opponent**. Both conditions give 2 VP; either alone gives 1 VP; neither gives none. Count cards in your deck and discard pile. Compare each opponent separately; if any one has at least as many as you, you do not meet the second condition, but may still score the first.
- **Count Ilban Richese / Countess Ariana Thorvald:** Ruthless Negotiator triggers only for paying the printed Solari cost of a board space, not a card ability costing Solari. Ariana’s Spice Addict is mandatory and affects only spice harvested by sending an Agent to a Maker space, not spice gained by other means.
- **Carryall / Liet Kynes:** original base spice is 1 at Imperial Basin, 2 at Hagga Basin and 3 at The Great Flat; accumulated bonus spice is not base spice. Liet Kynes counts qualifying cards from your Agent turns this round and your current Reveal turn, providing 2 Persuasion for each.
- **Helena Richese — Manipulate:** opponents cannot acquire the card you set aside. You may acquire it by another effect, but its 1-Persuasion discount does not apply then. If you have not acquired it by the end of your next Reveal turn, remove it from the game.
- **Dispatch an Envoy:** it adds only missing Faction Agent icons. Existing icons remain, including non-Faction icons; it never creates a duplicate icon.
- **Double Cross / Gun Thopter:** Double Cross requires at least one opponent troop in the Conflict, but does not require a troop in your own supply. Gun Thopter’s Agent box does not affect an opponent with no garrisoned troops.
- **Shifting Allegiances:** you may lose and gain Influence with the same Faction for a net gain of one. You must actually pay the one-Influence loss; a Faction where you have zero cannot pay it.
- **Recruitment Mission:** its acquisition destination choice applies only during your Reveal turn that round, not Agent-turn acquisitions. Choose independently for each card acquired whether it goes atop your deck or into your discard pile.
- **Refocus / Poison Snooper:** Refocus reshuffles your deck if your discard pile is empty. Cards drawn during a Reveal turn must immediately be revealed and used during that turn.
- **Missionaria Protectiva erratum:** it belongs to the Bene Gesserit Faction; that label is missing in the first English printing. After replacing misprints, include only two copies in the Imperium deck.

Game Overview and Major Concepts
Objective
You are a Leader of one of the Great Houses of the Landsraad. Defeat your rivals in Combat, wield political Influence, and form alliances with 
the four major Factions. Your successes will be measured in Victory Points.
Whenever you gain or lose a Victory Point, move your Score marker up or down one space on the Score track. At the end of a 
round, if any player has reached 10 or more Victory Points (or if the Conflict Deck is empty), the game ends, and whoever has the 
most Victory Points wins.
Leaders
Each Leader has two different unique abilities:
The first, on the left, is used during play as described on the Leader.
The second, on the right and marked by the Signet Ring icon, is activated when 
you play your Signet Ring card on one of your Agent turns.
Deck Building
You start the game with a 10-card deck containing the same cards as the other players. Adding to and changing that deck is the key element 
of play in a deck-building game. During each round, you may acquire new cards to add to your deck. Because cards do many different things, 
each player’s deck and strategy will diverge as the game unfolds.
Whenever you acquire a new Imperium or Reserve card, it is first placed in your discard pile. 
And any time you’re unable to draw a card because your deck is empty, you reshuffle your 
discard pile to form a new deck, then continue to draw as needed.
There are also ways to “trash” cards, removing them from your deck altogether for the rest of 
the game. By strategically removing weaker cards from your deck, you increase the chances of drawing your stronger cards more often.
Agents
You start the game with two Agents (and can gain a third 
during play). You send Agents to spaces on the game 
board, sometimes gathering resources, sometimes paying 
resources to advance your strategy. (This is explained fully 
in Phase 2: Player Turns, while board spaces are described in 
detail in the separate Board Space Guide sheet.)
In DUNE: IMPERIUM, Agents and cards are tightly linked; you can’t 
send an Agent to a board space without first playing a card that 
allows it.
The Mentat Agent
The Mentat is a special freelance Agent that 
you can temporarily add to your roster of 
Agents for one round. See the Mentat board 
space in the separate Board Space Guide sheet 
for more details.
Cards of any type can override 
the usual rules of the game!

Factions
In DUNE: IMPERIUM, the four Factions represent powerful forces on Dune and elsewhere in the Imperium. Increasing your Influence and 
earning an Alliance with one or more of them is one of the key routes to victory in the game. See “Across the Imperium” on Page 2 for short 
descriptions of each of the Factions.
 
 
 
Your Faction cubes begin at the bottom of each Faction’s Influence track. Throughout the game, your Influence 
with a Faction will increase or decrease, depending on the cards you play and the actions you take. When you 
send an Agent to a Faction’s board space, gain one Influence with that Faction by advancing your cube one 
space on its Influence track. Other game effects can also move your cube up (and occasionally down) the track.
When you reach 2 Influence with a Faction, you gain a Victory Point. If you drop back below 2 Influence, you lose 
that Victory Point.
When you reach 4 Influence, you earn the bonus shown on that space of the track. If you drop back below 4 
Influence, you do not give back the bonus. (It’s possible—though unusual—to earn the same bonus more than 
once, if you move back then advance again.)
The first player to reach 4 Influence with a Faction also earns an Alliance with that Faction. They take the Alliance 
token from the track, put it in their supply and gain the Victory Point shown on the Alliance token. If they are ever 
passed by an opponent rising to a higher space on the track, they must give the Alliance token to that opponent; 
they lose that Victory Point and the opponent gains it.
Intrigue Cards
Intrigue cards represent subterfuge, backroom dealings, and surprise twists—
they can provide resources like water or spice, increase your Influence with a 
Faction, or even score Victory Points. Each Intrigue card indicates when it can be 
played, what effect it has, and whether there are costs or conditions to playing it.
You receive Intrigue cards primarily from three board spaces: Carthag, Conspire, 
and Secrets. (But look for other opportunities on cards, wherever you see the 
Intrigue card icon.) They are kept face down, separate from your deck. You may 
look at them at any time. Reveal them to your opponents only when you play 
them. Once an Intrigue card is played and resolved, place it face up in a discard 
pile next to the Intrigue Deck.
There are three types of Intrigue cards: Plot, Combat, and Endgame.
You may play a Plot Intrigue card any time during one of your Agent or Reveal turns.
You may play a Combat Intrigue card only during Combat.
You may play an Endgame Intrigue card only at the end of the game.

There are three board spaces on Arrakis with a Maker 
icon, where you may harvest spice: The Great Flat, 
Hagga Basin, and Imperial Basin. When you send an 
Agent to one of them, you gain the base value of spice 
shown on the space, plus any bonus spice that has 
accumulated there. (See Phase 4: Makers for details.)
When you send an Agent to Hagga 
Basin, you gain 2 spice from the bank 
and take any bonus spice that has 
accumulated there.

John has no more Agents when his turn comes, so he 
takes a Reveal turn. He reveals the three cards remaining in 
his hand: Imperial Spy, Smuggler’s Thopter, and Stilgar.
Smuggler’s Thopter has an effect for John to resolve. 
He takes 1 spice from the bank. His cards also provide 
Persuasion and swords.
John’s cards give him a total of 4 Persuasion. He uses 3 of 
it to acquire Space Travel from the Imperium Row, placing 
it in his discard pile. A new card is then dealt from the 
Imperium Deck to fill the empty space in the Imperium Row. 
Although John has 1 Persuasion remaining, there are no 
cards available that cost only 1.
John has two troops in the Conflict, providing a total of 4 strength. The cards he revealed 
this turn provide 4 more: 1 sword from Imperial Spy and 3 swords from Stilgar. He sets his 
Combat marker at 8 on the Combat track.
Finally, John takes the cards in front of him and puts them in his discard pile.
The phase continues. Abby and Ned will take a Reveal turn at some point. John is done until 
the Combat phase.
When a player has no more Agents for Agent turns (or chooses not to use any Agents they have remaining), that player takes a Reveal turn. 
This consists of the following steps in order: Reveal Cards, Resolve Reveal Effects, Set Strength, and Clean Up.
Reveal Cards
Reveal all cards remaining in your hand, placing them 
face up in play in front of you. Keep them separate from 
other cards you played previously on Agent turns.
Resolve Reveal Effects
You now gain the effects in the Reveal boxes of all the 
cards you just revealed (but not those of any cards you 
played during Agent turns earlier in the round).
You may resolve Reveal effects in any 
order you like. In addition, you may 
use Persuasion that you’ve gained 
to acquire new cards for your deck 
before, between, or after your Reveal 
effects.
Set Strength
Total your strength for the Combat this round.
Each troop you have in the Conflict is worth 2 strength. 
(Troops in your garrison or supply contribute nothing.)
Each sword you revealed during your Reveal turn is 
worth 1 strength.
You must have at least one troop in the Conflict to 
have any strength. If your last troop is ever removed, 
your strength becomes 0, and can’t be increased by any 
means, including swords on cards you revealed.
When you’ve totaled your 
strength, announce it to 
your opponents and move 
your Combat marker to 
the corresponding space on the Combat track. If your 
strength is over 20, flip the Combat marker to the 
+20 side and start again from the beginning of the track.
Clean Up
Remove all the cards from in front of you (from your 
Agent and Reveal turns) and put them in your discard 
pile.
 Player Turn – Reveal Turn
Acquiring Cards
The Persuasion you gain during a round is used during your 
Reveal turn to acquire new cards for your deck. You may 
acquire any of the five cards in the Imperium Row, or Arrakis Liaison 
or The Spice Must Flow from the Reserve. (Foldspace is acquired at 
the board space of the same name, as described in the separate 
Board Space Guide sheet.)
The cost to acquire a card is shown at the top right of that card. 
You may acquire as many cards as you like, as long as you have 
enough Persuasion to spend. You may pool Persuasion from multiple 
sources (cards and board spaces) to acquire one card, and may split 
Persuasion from a single source to pay for different cards. Persuasion 
is not represented by any tokens because you can never save it; any 
Persuasion you don’t use during your Reveal turn is lost.
When you acquire a card, place it in your discard pile (face up to the 
right of your Leader). You don’t get to use the new card right away; 
you will shuffle it along with the rest of your discard pile when you 
run out of cards to draw.
The Imperium Row must always have five cards; whenever it does 
not, replace missing cards from the top of the Imperium Deck. This 
means that after you acquire one card, you may then acquire the 
card that replaces it (if you have enough Persuasion).

As the Combat Phase begins, John has 8 strength and Abby has 6 strength. John has the First Player marker, but he’s already ahead in the 
Conflict. He passes on the chance to play a Combat Intrigue card.
Abby is next, and does play an Intrigue card, Ambush. It gives her 4 more strength, and she advances her Combat marker to 10.
Ned is next in player order, but has no troops in the Conflict. He has 0 strength and can’t take part in this phase.
It’s now back to John. Even though he passed earlier in this phase, he could now decide to play an Intrigue card. But he checks his Intrigue 
cards, and none of them are Combat Intrigue cards. He passes again.
Abby, satisfied with her victory, also passes.
With 10 strength, Abby wins the Conflict. The top reward of the Conflict card, Siege of Arrakeen, gives her 1 Victory Point and control of 
Arrakeen. She advances her Score marker one space on the Score track, and places one of her Control markers on the flag below the Arrakeen 
board space.
John wins the second-place reward, taking 4 Solari from the bank.
Ned receives nothing from this Conflict. He has 0 strength, and the third-place reward isn’t available in a 3-player game anyway.
Combat is resolved during this phase, but first, players have the chance to play Combat Intrigue cards.
 Phase 3: Combat
Combat Intrigue Cards
Starting with the player who has the 
First Player marker and continuing 
clockwise, each player with at least 
one troop in the Conflict may play any 
number of Combat Intrigue cards, or 
may pass.
You are not required to pass just 
because you passed earlier in the 
Combat phase. Once all players 
involved in Combat pass consecutively, 
you then resolve the Combat.
If a card changes the number of troops a player has in 
the Conflict (or otherwise alters their strength), they 
adjust their Combat marker accordingly on the Combat 
track. (Remember: if you have no troops in the Conflict, 
your strength is 0.)
A few Combat Intrigue cards do something “when 
you win a Conflict.” You do not play these now, before 
resolving the Combat. Instead, wait until you’ve won, 
then play them (before moving on to the next phase).
Resolve Combat
Rewards from the Conflict card are given to players based on their 
strength, as shown on the Combat track.
The player with the highest strength wins the Conflict 
and gains the top reward on the Conflict card. 
The player with the second highest strength gains the 
second reward. In a 4-player game (only), the player 
with the third highest strength receives the third 
reward.
A player with 0 strength does not receive any reward.
Refer to this rulebook’s back cover for a guide to the 
icons used on Conflict cards.
Once all rewards have been given, each player takes their troops from 
the Conflict and puts them in their supply (not their garrison). Reset all 
Combat markers to 0 on the Combat track.
Ties
When players tie for first place, no one wins the Conflict. The tied 
players each receive the second reward. (In a 4-player game, if two 
players tie for first place, the other two players still compete for the 
third reward.)
When players tie for second place, they each receive the third reward.
Players tying for third place receive nothing.

If any player is at 10 or more Victory Points on the Score track, or if the Conflict Deck is 
empty, the Endgame is triggered.
If no one has won, prepare the next round:
Return the Mentat to its designated space in the Landsraad (if it’s not already there).
Players recall their Agents, returning them to their Leaders.
Pass the First Player marker clockwise to the next player, then begin a new 
round with Phase 1.
No one has reached 10 Victory Points, so the Mentat and the player Agents are returned to the appropriate 
places, and the First Player marker passes clockwise to Abby. A new round then begins, with phase 1.
In this phase, spice can accumulate on certain board spaces. Check each of the three board spaces with a Maker icon: The Great Flat, 
Hagga Basin, and Imperial Basin. If the space does not have an Agent, place 1 spice from the bank on that space (in the spot designated for 
bonus spice). This spice is added to any bonus spice that may already be there from previous rounds.
There is an Agent in Imperial Basin. (John played it there earlier this round.) There are no Agents in the Great Flat or Hagga Basin, 
however, so each of those spaces gets 1 bonus spice. The Great Flat already had 1 bonus spice from a previous round, so now it has 2 
bonus spice.
 Phase 4: Makers
 Phase 5: Recall
Endgame
First, you may play and resolve any 
Endgame Intrigue cards you have. 
Then whoever has the most Victory 
Points is declared the winner.
If the case of a tie, tiebreakers are, 
in order: amount of spice, Solari, 
water, and garrisoned troops.

choose two of the four Baron Harkonnen tokens and place them on

card, then immediately end your turn.

card. (You may also play To the Victor… to gain the spice to then

even if you have no Agents left in your supply, as it lets you send

back to the space that it was just on.
If a board space can be used only once per game (High Council, 
Swordmaster), you can’t use Kwisatz Haderach to send an Agent 
there more than once. You can’t overcome The Voice and send an 
Agent to a board space where you can’t send an Agent.
If you move an agent away from a space with a Maker icon, 
and that space remains empty until Phase 4, bonus spice does 
accumulate there.
Paul Atreides / Poison Snooper — You can’t look at the top card of 
your deck if it is empty. (You can’t reshuffle your discard pile and 
form a new deck until you need to draw a card.)

your left and proceeding clockwise. Each opponent must choose 
something they can do; they can’t discard if their hand is empty, or 
lose a deployed troop if they have none. An opponent who decides 
to discard chooses which card; it is not random.
The Voice — Use one of your available Control markers to mark 
the board space you choose, then remove it on your next turn. 
(The Voice only stops opponents from sending Agents to that 
board space for one turn.)
This does prevent Kwisatz Haderach from sending an Agent to the 
board space you chose.

House Hagal cards are used to control automated opponents (hereafter referred to as “Rivals”) who 
compete against you in solo and two-player games. These opponents send Agents to occupy board 
spaces and contest Conflicts by recruiting and deploying troops.
Rivals are affected by cards and board spaces that affect opponents (or “players”), if they have the 
specified resources.
Agents
During Phase 2: Player Turns, a Rival will take Agent turns but it will not take Reveal turns.
When a Rival takes an Agent turn, reveal the top card of the House Hagal deck. That card will send an Agent to the revealed board space, as long as that space is 
unoccupied. If the space is occupied, ignore the card and continue revealing cards until you reveal an unoccupied space.
If the House Hagal deck is ever empty (or if the Reshuffle card is revealed), immediately reshuffle the House Hagal cards to form a new deck.
When a Rival sends an Agent to a board space, ignore all normal costs and effects of that space. Instead, it gets only the effects indicated on its revealed card:
The Rival advances on the indicated Influence 
track. It earns no bonuses from an Influence 
track, but it will take a Faction Alliance if able.
The Rival uses the Signet Ring ability on its Leader. (Solo Play only)
The Rival recruits one troop from its supply for each such icon. If the 
revealed card is a Combat space, deploy them to the Conflict. 
Otherwise, put the troops in its garrison.
Any time a Rival sends an Agent to a Combat space, it also deploys up to two 
troops from its garrison (if available) to the Conflict. Do this even if the card itself 
recruited no troops (for example: a Harvest Spice card).
Combat
When Phase 3: Combat begins, each Rival that has at least one troop in the Conflict gets a Combat bonus. In turn order, reveal the top card of the House Hagal deck. (If you 
reveal the Reshuffle card, follow the instructions to reshuffle the deck and reveal again.) Ignore everything on the revealed card except for the sword icons at the bottom. 
Advance the opponent’s Combat marker on the Combat track by the number of swords revealed. Players may then play Combat Intrigue cards before resolving Combat.
House Hagal Cards — Solo & Two-Player Games
Harvest Spice cards
If the revealed card is a Harvest Spice card, 
follow the instructions on the card. If the card 
sends a Rival’s Agent to harvest spice, remove 
any bonus spice on the space. (In a two-player 
game, return it to the bank. When playing Solo, 
follow the Solo Play rules for Harvesting Spice.)
In a two-player game, a third, Rival player, House Hagal, competes against you and your opponent, serving a spoiler role. It operates by its own set of rules. It doesn’t collect 
resources, build a deck, earn rewards, or score Victory Points. It does, however, use the House Hagal cards as described earlier, sending Agents to occupy board spaces and 
competing in Conflicts by recruiting and deploying troops.
During the Game
After each of the First Player’s Agent turns, House Hagal acts, as long as it has an Agent remaining in its 
supply. (Use the method described earlier) The number of turns that House Hagal takes each round will 
vary because it acts after the First Player. For example, if one player has a Swordmaster and the other does 
not, it might take three turns in one round, then two in the next.
Because House Hagal can’t collect rewards from a Conflict, it can never claim control of a board space. 
However, if it wins a Conflict for a board space currently controlled by another player, remove that player’s 
Control marker.

on each of the bottom spaces beneath the Influence

During Phase 2: Player Turns, your Rivals each take Agent turns in sequence with you, as long as they have an Agent remaining in their supply. (Use the method described

When a Rival uses Harvest Spice to send an Agent to a board space, it gains all spice there (base and bonus). Place any accumulated resources in the Rival’s supply.
Combat
Rivals gain first- and second-place rewards from Conflicts, even things they otherwise don’t take from board spaces:
They gain Victory Points, and Influence with Factions.
They gain Solari, Spice, Water, and Intrigue cards. Keep these in the Rival’s supply (to be spent as indicated below).
They win Control of board spaces, placing a Control marker on the flag below it. On future turns, they get the Control bonus whenever you or a Rival sends an Agent

They gain the Mentat, and use it as an Agent during the next round.

At **4 Influence** you earn the bonus shown on that space of the track; you do *not* give the bonus back if you later drop below 4, and you can even earn it again by dropping back and re-advancing.
   164	- **Alliances:** the **first** player to reach 4 Influence with a Faction takes its Alliance token and gains the VP shown on it. If an opponent ever passes them by rising to a **higher** space on that track, the token (and its VP) transfers to that opponent. Merely tying the holder does not take it. If the holder loses Influence while previously tied with another player, the previously tied player takes it; if several were tied, the holder chooses one. The holder also loses the token if falling to 3 Influence or less: if no player has 4 or more to take it, return it to the board. Every Alliance ownership change immediately moves **both** affected scores: the former holder loses its 1 VP and the new holder gains 1 VP; returning it to the board just loses the former holder's VP.
   165	- **Mentat:** a freelance Agent. Take it only from its space on the board (you can't take it from another player or another space), place it on your Leader, and use it as one of your Agents this round; return it to its Landsraad space during Recall. For the Sort Through the Chaos Conflict reward, take the Mentat at the start of the next round and use it that round (official FAQ timing).
   166	- **Swordmaster & High Council** are once-per-game spaces for each player (8 Solari for your third Agent; 5 Solari for a Council seat granting 2 Persuasion every Reveal turn).

   168	- **Deck exhaustion:** any time you're unable to draw because your deck is empty, reshuffle your discard pile to form a new deck, then continue drawing. You can't reshuffle early — e.g., Paul Atreides' ability or Poison Snooper can't look at the top card of an empty deck.

   170	- **Losing vs. retreating troops:** a **lost** troop returns to your supply (not your garrison); a **retreated** troop moves from the Conflict back to your garrison. If an effect permits retreating “any number,” zero is allowed.

   183	### Two-player House Hagal Rival
   184	
   185	House Hagal is a third, spoiler Rival in every standard two-player game. It does not collect resources, build an Imperium deck, earn Conflict rewards or score VP, and cannot claim Control. It can take and hold Faction Alliances, denying their VP to humans. It is affected by effects targeting opponents or players if it has the specified resources.
   186	
   187	**Setup:** choose an unused color. Put one of its cubes at the bottom of each of the four Influence tracks; all remaining cubes go in its supply, with **no troops in its garrison**. Remove the three Arrakeen cards marked “1P,” shuffle the remaining House Hagal cards and put the deck and its **three Agents** near its supply. No Rival Leader or solo difficulty rules are used.
   188	
   189	**Agent turns:** after each of the **First Player’s Agent turns**, House Hagal takes one Agent turn if it has an Agent left in supply. A Swordmaster gives that First Player a third Agent and can allow a third Agent turn, so House Hagal may take **three turns instead of two**. Its actual count follows the First Player’s actual Agent turns and House Hagal’s remaining Agents, with a maximum of three Rival turns per round. It does not act after the other human’s turn or after a Reveal turn. There is **no fixed two-turn limit without a Swordmaster**: a temporary Mentat or recalled Agent may also allow another First Player Agent turn; early Revealing may reduce the count. It never takes a Reveal turn. Recall its Agents to its supply for the next round.
   190	
   191	Reveal the top House Hagal card and send an Agent to the indicated space if unoccupied; otherwise keep revealing until an eligible unoccupied space appears. If a card shows two spaces, use only the option matching the current conditions: if that option is occupied, draw a new card, never switch to the other option. Immediately reshuffle the House Hagal cards if the deck is empty or the Reshuffle card appears; continue revealing as needed.
   192	
   193	Ignore the normal costs, requirements and effects of the space. Resolve only the revealed card’s icons and instructions. Any time it sends an Agent to a Combat space, **automatically deploy two more garrison troops if available, one if only one is available, or none if the garrison is empty**. This deployment is mandatory for the automated Rival, even if the card recruited none; humans do not choose to hold its available troops back.
